title: Humility
hook: humility is taking your rightful space, no more and no less

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mendel of Satanov's method: one trait a week, a short line by day, a mark at night. Did you write your trait down somewhere? Today, the first trait on our walk through his kind of list. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-six.

Two people in the same meeting. One talks through every pause, takes every credit, fills every silence. The other sits in the corner with the answer everyone needs and never says it, because who are they to speak? Ask the room which one is humble, and the corner may well get the vote. Jewish teachers of character would push back. Both have the measure wrong. One takes too much space. The other takes too little, and the room loses what they had to give. Today's trait sits between them.
screen: `ONE FILLS EVERY SILENCE.` → `ONE NEVER SAYS THE ANSWER.` → `BOTH HAVE THE MEASURE WRONG.`

segments.voice: Anavah. Humility. Turn it four ways. First, Moses. The Torah, in the book of Numbers, calls Moses very meek, more than anyone on the face of the earth. That's the same Moses who stood before Pharaoh, carried the tablets down the mountain and argued with God on behalf of his people. So whatever humility means in this tradition, it doesn't mean shrinking. The humblest man in the Torah's own description took up a great deal of room, when the room needed him. Second, the prophet Micah. Asked what God requires, Micah answers with three things, and the last is to "walk humbly with thy God." Walk. Humility there is a way of moving through the world, not a feeling about yourself. Third, two pockets. A story is told about the Hasidic teacher Rabbi Simcha Bunim. He said a person should carry two slips of paper, one in each pocket. One says: for my sake the world was created, a line from the Mishnah. The other says: I am but dust and ashes, the words of Abraham in Genesis. The trick is knowing which pocket to reach into. When you're about to stay silent while someone is wronged, the first pocket. When you're about to take more than your share, the second. Fourth, the measure. That's why some Mussar teachers describe anavah as being right-sized. Not too large, crowding everyone out. Not too small, hiding a gift the room needs. A humble person, in this picture, isn't the one thinking little of themselves. It's the one thinking accurately, then making room for others. Yesterday's method gives a trait a week. Humility makes a good one to start with, because every other trait needs it to stay honest.
screen: `MOSES: VERY MEEK, AND NOT SMALL.` · `WALK HUMBLY: A WAY OF MOVING.` · `TWO SLIPS, TWO POCKETS.` · `NOT TOO LARGE, NOT TOO SMALL.` · then, large: `RIGHT-SIZED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take the right amount of space. Settle, and breathe. Start with your body. Are you slumped small, or spread wide? Let your seat be just what you need: feet on the floor, back long, shoulders easy. Now picture the next conversation you'll have today. Ask which pocket you'll need. Is there something true you usually swallow? Let yourself picture saying it, plainly. Or do you usually take over? Picture leaving one pause open for someone else. If you pray, you can carry this before God in your own words. If you don't, simply sit right-sized, and let that be enough. The bell holds the time.
Anavah. Humility: in Mussar, being right-sized, taking the space that is yours, no more and no less. Today's word.
Your line: right-sized. Today, in one conversation, notice whether you're too big or too small, and adjust by one step: speak once more, or once less. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: In Mussar practice, Jews working on anavah watch how much space they take in conversations and in their homes, sometimes keeping the two-pocket teaching of Rabbi Simcha Bunim as a reminder.

what it means: right-sized: the space that is yours, no more and no less.
what a scholar hears: Moses called very meek in Numbers, and Simcha Bunim's two pockets: the Mishnah's for my sake, and Abraham's dust and ashes.

sources.ref: Story told of Rabbi Simcha Bunim of Peshischa (two slips of paper)

notes: Micah 6:8 quoted as 'walk humbly with thy God' (JPS 1917, same in KJV); confirm.
Numbers 12:3 paraphrased ('very meek, more than anyone on the face of the earth'); 'the humblest man in the Torah's own description' rests on that verse. Confirm.
Simcha Bunim's two slips told as 'a story is told'; the lines are paraphrased from Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 and Genesis 18:27.
'Some Mussar teachers describe anavah as being right-sized' reflects contemporary Mussar teaching (e.g. Alan Morinis's phrasing); confirm it is fair and not too tied to one teacher.
Original: עֲנָוָה; the note says Moses is called anav in Numbers 12:3. Confirm.
